title: COLLINS, David. AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY IN NEW SOUTH WALES: with Remarks on the Dispositions, Customs, Manners, &c.
description: COLLINS, David. AN ACCOUNT OF THE ENGLISH COLONY IN NEW SOUTH WALES: with Remarks on the Dispositions, Customs, Manners, &c. of the Native Inhabitants of that Country. To which are added, some particulars of New Zealand; compiled, by permission, from the Mss. of Lieutenant-Governor King… Quarto, with a chart, folding map, 18 plates, and four engraved vignettes in the text, a good copy with intermittent paper toning, an early repair to the folding chart, bound without the half-title in last century chocolate morocco, slight shelf rubbing, recent owner’s label. London, T. Cadell and W. Davies, 1798. First edition: with contemporary signature of Wm. Scott, and three pencilled text notes (two of them initialled) of his connections to naval fleets and officers. The National Library of Scotland holds journals and logs of a William Scott in Penang 17941819. When published in 1798, this fine volume was intended to stand as a complete work, recording events from the preparations for the First Fleet expedition in 1786 up to Collins’s own departure from the colony in 1796. It is a detailed and informed account, with illustrations considered to be after sketches by Thomas Watling, offering a topographically accurate picture of the Sydney and Parramatta landscape in the 1790s. A further supplementary second volume was published in 1802. Davidson, pp. 90-2; Ferguson, 263; Hill 2, 335; Wantrup, 19. Estimate $1500/2000

title: HUNTER, John. AN HISTORICAL JOURNAL of the Transactions at Port Jackson and Norfolk Island, with the discoveries which h
description: HUNTER, John. AN HISTORICAL JOURNAL of the Transactions at Port Jackson and Norfolk Island, with the discoveries which have been made in New South Wales and in the Southern Ocean, since the publication of Phillip’s Voyage... Quarto, frontispiece, engraved title-page, plates and folding maps, an uncut copy in papered boards of the period, re-backed at an early date, retaining the original spine, with leather spine label. London, John Stockdale, 1793. First edition: a handsome copy (with wide margins) of this ‘official’ First Fleet narrative, written by the second governor, which continues Phillip’s 1789 Voyage as the official account of the first years of settlement at Sydney. Hunter gives an excellent account of many activities, particularly exploration and the settlement at Norfolk Island (based on Philip Gidley King’s papers), which are treated more cursorily by the other First Fleet chroniclers. The engraved plates and maps, many of the latter from original cartography by Hunter, Dawes and Bradley, are very fine. Among other plates – most notably William Blake’s engraving of an Aboriginal family after a drawing by Philip Gidley King – is the first published view of the First Fleet settlement at Sydney Cove, engraved by Edward Dayes after a drawing by Hunter. The view shows the settlement at Sydney Cove at the very earliest stage of its development. Davidson, pp. 87-9 (“essential”); Ferguson, 152; Hill 2, 857; McCormick, First Views, plate 7ff; Wantrup, 13. Estimate $3000/5000

title: GILES, Ernest. MR. E. GILES’S EXPLORATIONS, 18734 [drop title].
description: GILES, Ernest. MR. E. GILES’S EXPLORATIONS, 18734 [drop title]. Foolscap folio, pp. 69, large folding lithographed Map of the Country West of the Telegraph Line, re-sewn in early blue wrappers (spine gone). [Adelaide, Government Printer, 1874]. Rare: the first edition of Giles’s journal of his second – and arguably best remembered – expedition and his second attempt to conquer the western interior. The loss of Gibson in the course of this expedition and Giles’s heroic search for him is one of the inspiring, tragic episodes of Australian exploration. This is the first publication of Giles’s journal and, indeed, his first published work of any sort: the journal of his first expedition was not published until the following year. South Australian Parliamentary Paper no. 215. Gill, p. 13; McLaren 8989. Estimate $1000/2000

title: ROBERTSON (pseudonym).
description: ROBERTSON (pseudonym). VOYAGE DE ROBERTSON, AUX TERRES AUSTRALES, traduit sur le Manuscrit Anglois. Duodecimo, pp. [iv], 474, with the half-title; bound in continental calf of the epoch, a little rubbed; in a custommade box. Amsterdam [i.e. Paris], 1766. First edition, the rare first issue dated 1766, of an important and somewhat neglected Australian utopian novel. The supposed English author sailed with Francis Drake to South America in 1585. When land was sighted in the Pacific, Robertson was sent with a small cutter to investigate. Lost with his men in a sudden storm he was instead washed up on the shores of the large continent of Australia, where he discovered a plentiful, well-governed land. A satire on contemporary European society, the “narrative is supposed to have inspired William Penn to found an ideal settlement in North America” (Moors). The first edition sheets were subsequently re-issued with new preliminaries dated 1767. To judge by the marked rarity of this 1766 first issue, this took place not long after publication. Davidson, p. 43-4; Gove, p. 355; Hordern House IV, 51; Mackaness, 9; Moors, 24 (1767 issue/edition); Robert, 757. Estimate $1200/2400 received very well. Copies were evidently demanded back from the schools and the police are said to have seized copies held by a distributor. “The ‘problem’, was two photos, from Victoria of normal implements, which were considered by tribal Aborigines in the Western Australian bush to look like ‘secret’ items. There were many complaints, but to no avail and the copies were pulped in 2004” (Peter J. Bridges). Cains 77. Estimate $200/300

Sydney, Printed for the Author, of 2 Crown Street, Sydney, by Sydney Dorning Smith, of 194 Glebe Road, Glebe Point, at his Printery, No. 200 Castlereagh Street, May 1914. Rare: one of several Sydney editions published between 1912 and 1914 of this famous work, pleading for radical reform of the highly taboo subject of human sexuality. Chidley so sincerely believed that his theory of natural coition, natural dress and natural diet was mankind’s only hope for salvation that he submitted himself to all the indignities and persecution that late Victorian intolerance could bring to bear. His book condemned and destroyed, himself arrested, fined, incarcerated and eventually committed to an asylum where he died within a few years, Chidley remained to the last obsessively defiant. The three (or more) Sydney editions of 1912-14, although printed in large numbers, sold cheaply – indeed given away – over a period of years, are nonetheless rare today. It was for these Sydney printings that Chidley was prosecuted and his book banned. Cains 24 Estimate $100/200

Harcourt published his controversial second novel in 1934, a socialist realist novel written in the orthodox Marxist idiom then current. Complete with caricature Communist agitators (heroic not to say angelic), magistrates, businessmen, and police (malevolent all) and purported to describe the effects of the depression in Western Australia. Unlike the dull and tedious post-war propagandist ‘novels’ of fellow-Communist K.S. Prichard, Harcourt leavened his work with sex – what one contemporary reviewer described as “the bold course of giving his story an overpowering taint of the sexual”. Of course, sex sells but it also attracted the attention of police in both Western Australia and New South Wales and, finally, the Commonwealth authorities who banned it in November 1934, a little over six months after it was published. While the book’s sexual content and Communist advocacy aroused controversy in equal measure, it was banned only on the grounds of indecency and not lifted until 1958. It is a book rarely seen, not just because it was banned here but also because most English novels of this period have survived in much smaller numbers than they would have otherwise were it not for wartime paper drives, the Blitz, and all the other threats to survival in the following decade. In his inimitable, amusing, and possibly libellous style, Griffin relates at length how he was only able to see a copy of the book half-an-hour before the launch. He immediately saw that the printer had transposed pages, positioned text improperly, and generally made the book unacceptable. After a heated discussion between artist, publisher, and gallery owner, he found himself and his books on the street. He states that all copies were guillotined apart from his own that was later extensively marked up and pasted up for the correct second edition of 1980 (Richard Griffin’s copy, James Hardie Library, State Library of Queensland). It is evident that the eccentric Griffin was too aggravated, in his self-dramatising way, to notice that Klepac had palmed a copy, and maybe the others did too. So, while Griffin’s copy is indeed unique by virtue of his annotation, it is clearly not the only copy in existence. Cains 135. Estimate $500/800
